segments.text: Cursors: walking through the rows of a query, one at a time.
S Q L works on whole sets. One UPDATE changes every matching row at once.
But sometimes a program must visit the rows one at a time, and do something different with each.
That is what a cursor is for: a pointer over the result of a query, like a finger running down the class list.
You have already used cursors without knowing it. Oracle opens an implicit cursor for every INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE.
After this update, S Q L percent row count says how many rows changed: just one, the Python grade.
And S Q L percent found says whether any did.
An explicit cursor has a fixed lifecycle. First, declare it: give it a name and its query.
OPEN runs the query. The result is ready, and the pointer waits before the first row.
Inside a loop, each FETCH copies the current row into the record r, and moves the pointer down one row.
After the last row, FETCH finds nothing. The NOTFOUND attribute becomes true, and EXIT WHEN leaves the loop.
Finally, CLOSE frees the cursor.
Every cursor has four attributes. ISOPEN says whether it is open. FOUND is true when the last FETCH returned a row, and NOTFOUND when it found nothing.
ROWCOUNT counts the rows fetched so far. For the implicit cursor, write S Q L in front.
Writing OPEN, FETCH, EXIT and CLOSE every time is tedious. The cursor FOR loop does all four for you.
The record r is declared automatically, the loop stops after the last row, and the cursor is always closed, even after an error.
Now a real task. A teacher curves the grades, with a rule per course: in Databases, low grades gain one point or half a point; in Statistics, everyone gains a point.
FOR UPDATE locks the selected rows until the commit, so nobody changes them halfway through.
And WHERE CURRENT OF updates exactly the row under the pointer.
Four becomes five, six and a half becomes seven, and in Statistics, nine and a half stops at ten.
A common mistake: writing a cursor loop when one UPDATE would do.
If each row only needs a formula on its own values, a single set-based statement changes the whole table at once, and much faster.
Keep cursors for work one statement cannot express: several steps per row, procedure calls, or decisions that depend on earlier rows.
Practise it in the SQL section of the course site.
